I have well over 2000 hours in Borderlands 2 over all platforms and have been playing it for over a decade, and I can say that it is probably my overall favorite game every and I highly recommend it to anyone. I recently got a PC and started playing modded BL2 and it lead me to writing this review for it. 

Positives:

BL2 has a great story main that is quite replayable, with many great NPCs with the vault hunters from borderlands 1 retuning as NPCs, and an absolutely amazing main antagonist with Handsome Jack. Handsome Jack is such a good villain and character in general, he is written great and his voice actor does an amazing job conveying Jacks emotion and really gets you invested in his character. Jack is charismatic, funny, and confident, with deep story beats and traits that make you love and hate him. 

The playable characters in this game do not disappoint. Each of them are very unique, not only visually but in personality and gameplay. I am sure that among the 6 different vault hunter you will find at least one that fits your playstyle. 

The visuals are very good. The game is older and it is supposed to be a "graphical" game in the first place, but despite that the world is still full of great quality visuals, and I personally love the cell shaded comic book look to the world. It add character and a uniqueness to the game that you don't always find, especially in modern days with game always trying to push realism and peak graphics. Some people might not like the more cartoony look, but I think it is great and fits the game perfectly. 

The loot is great. This is a looter shooter after all, so the most important part is the loot. There are so many guns in this game, with high end rarities of legendary, pearlescent, and seraph, the amount of different design guns is incredible. Many powerful options to choose from and they often have very interest quirks such as very specific firing patterns or other abilities. There is even many unique mission reward weapons that are some of the most powerful in the game and are staples on multiple builds. 

The DLCs are all great (I do actually enjoy Hammerlocks DLC, not as good as the other but still good). Each DLC offers a very different story with new interesting characters and character from the main story, a complete change of scenery, and of course new weapons and other gear pieces to farm and play with. Even the headhunter packs are good and are nice short stories. 

Community. The borderlands community is very lively and while the current franchise doesn't please everybody, their are still many people playing the older games such as youtubers like JoltzDude and others. The modding community is also great with new mods coming out to this day and so many more already released that overhaul weapons skill trees or do simply thing like cutscene skip for auto pick up items. If you have played the game before I highly recommend trying some mods, they can revitalize your interest in the game. 

Negatives:

There are many positives to BL2 but there is some negatives as well. 

End Game Balancing. The end game balancing is fairly bad. Normal enemies and mobbing might not be terrible if you have a good build but there are many enemies that are bullet sponges if you don't have amazing gear, and this issue get worse when bossing and much worse when fight the end game bosses or Invincibles. Many builds if they are not perfect simply don't have the DPS or survivability to do the late game bosses with out lots of prep with certain skills, a little luck with certain skills, or glitching/ abusing certain interactions. I suppose it is the highest level of difficulty so it makes sense that most people won't be able to put the time and effort in to get perfect gear or learn certain mechanics to make a kill more efficient. 

This issue leads to the the next one and that is builds diversity. Every character has basically one viable late game build besides Salvador that can kinda use anything because he is a walking glitch. Character do have multiple builds but at late game they just fall off heavily for different reasons. for example Zero's melee build fall off a ton because melee damage just simply isn't well balanced in this game, heck even in the current game BL4 melee may be good but it isn't exactly "balanced". These other builds might not work well in end game but they can easily work and feel strong during the leveling process and playing through the main story, so if you don't want to play endgame then this really isn't an issue for you. 

In conclusion Borderlands 2 is the staple looter shooter and is an amazing game that has a good story, good characters, a great villain, good playable characters, worth while DLC, good loot, great level design and visuals, and fun gameplay, and a great modding community that can give the game new life for players who have been playing for a long time. I highly recommend to people familiar with RPG looter shooter games or anyone looking for something new and hasn't played this game before.

Borderlands 2 is the sequel to the idea pitched in the mid-aughts of 'What if Diablo II had guns?' to which every person at Gearbox software replied in unison 'It would #@%&ing rule!' and opted to work tirelessly to make this dream a reality. Though my hour-count on Steam is only 80 or so hours, I have probably two thousand more on the Xbox 360 played exclusively on Maya... not even to OP8 or anything. 

The art style is refined from the first game and shockingly vibrant and varied for a late-7th generation game. To go from Borderlands (2009)'s atmospheric, desaturated, and dingy Pandora to Borderlands 2's is the ideal way to expand on a universe without taking away from what makes it so hellish. Even environments returning from BL1 manage to have new pops of color that make them stand out... it's just a shame that they're so few and so late into the game that they aren't given the time to sit with you. 

In terms of gameplay, it's largely an objective improvement. Item parts have been standardized and made far more memorable such that an experienced player can identify if a piece of gear is a godroll before they ever view the item card; a mechanic I believe future games drop the ball on in favor of more variation. Gunplay is different to a degree, but probably really only because of the shift in engine from 1 to 2, but skills are vastly improved. Like the previous game, each of the four Vault Hunters (six if you have the DLC) feature wholly unique action skills and three skill trees, allowing for specialization and hybrid playstyles with the new action skill augments and melee overrides.

The last thing I feel is worth mentioning is the soundtrack. Borderlands 2 features heavily on electronic tracks while retaining some of the western ambient music from the previous title, fusing into a pretty fun tonal clash that never really feels grating. Combat music gives way to ambience naturally, and exploration is made all the better for it. I think the one thing Borderlands has consistently excelled in is music and setting the tone of their games appropriately with it.

I was going to write a well-thought out review to this game, but since it's Borderlands, here's a list of enemies whose designers I sincerely hope never find gainful employment in the video games industry ever again.

Rakks: Flying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that frequently get stuck inside your hitbox, causing the game to register millions of damage, instantly depleting your shield and putting you at 10% HP.

Buzzards: Tanky flying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that move around like they're being piloted by someone that's simultaneously drunk and on crack. Way too much HP, way too hard to hit, and spawn way too often.

Surveryors: Flying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (are you seeing a theme here?) that also move around like their AI is being piloted by someone that's simultaneously drunk and on crack. Shoots electrical bolts at you that deplete your shields before flying away to Tanzania for approximately 3 business days.

Stalkers: The developer that thought giving a small, hypermobile, hard to hit mob, access to invisibility that it spams quite literally every 0.2 seconds needs a psychiatric evaluation.

Loaders (of all kinds): Extremely tanky. Take 3 steps in any Hyperion-controlled territory and you're going to get assaulted by at least a dozen of these. Their weak point is literally a single red dot on their chassis that is absurdly difficult to hit, and even worse, some variants (BUL Loaders and Power Loaders) cover their weak spots.

Rats: Extremely erratic movement makes it almost impossible to land clean headshots on them. They also steal your loot and hit like an absolute truck for no reason. Also has a fun habit of running away whenever you get close and digging into the ground to escape.

Threshers: Whack-a-mole, except the moles can lob highly damaging projectiles at you, burrow into the ground the second you even think about approaching them or have them within your crosshairs, and some can even hit you from under your feet by sending burrowing tentacles.

Marauders: Simple foot soldiers that seem harmless until you get downed into FFYL mode. When that happens, they immediately bolt away to Uganda in order to deny you second wind. Also I swear their AI makes it so that the moment you have them in your crosshairs, they'll duck under cover for approximately 8 hours.

Nomads: So tanky and for why? Tiny head hitbox makes aiming for headshots on these guys absolutely miserable. Also why do they move around like that despite being so bulky?

And all of this is before encountering "Rabid" variants of these enemies, which I hear are a hundred times worse. Of course, this can all be mitigated very easily by playing in a group, which the game is practically SCREAMING for you to do, but if you choose to play this game solo, you have been warned. 7/10.

With just these two play through's you could get a character up to max level at the time (level 50). Then they added the first DLC which added more content, then the second DLC which added more and more and more. Then they added new game ++. Then there was the level cap upgrades which took the max level to 61 then 72 then 80 if you get all the DLC. Then there was the the head hunter packs which were micro DLC's which didn't add that much but still more content. It got to the point where taking a character to max level and do all three playthroughs takes around 80 hours. Nothing wrong with that but after playing the story twice the third gets really stale. 

The game is still good but wait for a sale and get everthing all at once for cheap.

[b]Summary[/b]
They just don't make games like this anymore.  This is not a perfect game, far from it, but there is a massive amount of content offered that is varied, entertaining, and very replayable.  You don't need to create an account (unless you want SHIFT codes), you can play it offline or online, and it rewards you the more you play with permanent stat buffs to all of your characters (which can be toggled, as good games offer).

[b]The Good[/b]
First off, if you're a nerd there are a bazillion and one references to random properties.  You'll likely never understand them all, though there are YouTube videos that attempt to if you're interested.  My favourite is the Goliaths referencing the old X-Men arcade game where Magneto addresses your party with the classic 'Welcome to die!' line.

I mentioned the mountains of content, and while it's difficult to explain the bottom line is that there is at least as much DLC content as there is in the main game.  The big DLCs alone will take several hours each to get through, and that's ignoring the side quests.  They are also unique with a pirate-themed campaign, a dungeons & dragons inspired one, and so on.  There's unique gear to be found as well.  Plus smaller DLCs.  There's so much here.

The looter shooter aspect works very well, it's essentially unchanged since the 1990s when Diablo was doing random loot drops of various rarities for taking down enemies.  It's not broken, so don't fix it.  You'll slowly collect a second currency called Eridium that lets you expand your inventory and maximum ammo supplies (as well as other things down the road).

The badass point system is something I've really come to appreciate.  You gain badass 'rank' for doing almost anything (shooting a certain number of bullets, taking down a certain number of enemies, finding secrets, completing quests, using all the character classes, etc, etc, etc.).  As your rank increases the game will award points you can spend to permanently upgrade all of your characters, even ones you haven't created yet.  These upgrades include gun damage, shield capacity, improved chances at triggering elemental effects, and many other useful stat boosts.  Every new character gets a clean slate of badass rank to gain; it's executed incredibly well.

All of the character classes play very differently, but don't really restrict you in terms of using whatever weapons or strategies you want.  There are classes that can lean in certain directions, for example the Commando can get additional assault rifle damage or the Assassin that has a whole skill tree dedicated to sniping.

[b]The Bad[/b]
The big one here is stability.  It runs fine the vast majority of the time, but it will crash on you.  Especially if you have the HD Texture pack installed, but I've had it crash without that installed as well.  When it does crash, unfortunately, it is very rarely clean and a crash to desktop.  Instead the game will just lock up after several hours for seemingly random reasons, and a lot of those times you'll just need to CTRL+ALT+DEL and restart your PC.  If it runs out of video memory, it will usually give you a message that you can click where it will reliably crash to desktop.

The 2 stickiest points for me are Sanctuary and Opportunity.  I've started a character and played through to the first time you get to Sanctuary.  If I don't quit and restart once I get to Sanctuary, the game will reliably crash when I go to Zed's and the game attempts to show me his intro cutscene.  Opportunity I have no idea why it locks up so frequently; uninstalling the HD Texture pack does seem to reduce crashes here.  Sometimes the game locks up within 30 seconds of me going to Opportunity, other times I can complete every single quest it has to offer in one sitting without issue.

If you want to play with friends online you should know that the MacOS and Windows versions of the game are different.  It looks like the Windows version got an update that never came to MacOS, and as such you will not be able to see or play with friends online if you're on different OSs (even if you're both using Steam and are friends).  There are workarounds online which basically involve reverting Windows installs to a previous, compatible version.  This seems like a pretty blatant oversight, and it's unfortunate that this issue likely won't ever be fixed by Gearbox.

[b]The Ugly[/b]
Borderlands 2 wasn't born ugly, it's more like it will accumulate little scars and imperfections the more you play it.  That said, the biggest scar is how much the terrain will get in your way.  You will get stuck and think you've soft-locked yourself at points.  You will wonder why your character can't go up some stairs without needing to jump on the staircase first.  If you try to walk forward for more than about 20 seconds in a straight line, you will probably get snagged and stuck on some piece of terrain.  Should you drive on a road, your car will randomly get stopped dead or flung way off the track when two segments of the road meet.  It's rarely a big deal, but when it happens during a boss fight or racing mission?  Straight up ugly.

The other big scar doesn't matter until after you've beaten the first two difficulty loops, and I would argue at this point you've probably gotten your money's worth out of the game.  You might disagree if you insist on only playing a single character.  The final difficulty level essentially requires you to have identically levelled characters, as whoever has the highest level in your party sets the bar for monster/loot levels.  Did you finish the second loop at level 50 while your friend finished it at level 55?  Well, too bad for you, everything will be level 55 if you both hop into the third loop.  A difference of 5 levels might not sound like much, but at this point everything scales so quickly your gear is effectively useless if it's 3 or more levels behind you.  Enemies are also buffed so much that you require slag element damage.  That's fine for a couple classes - like the Commando who can drop turrets with slag ammo - but for other classes it means constantly switching gear so you can slag something and actually have a chance at taking it down.

Now for the smaller scars.  There have been multiple times where I haven't been able to join friends' games or vice versa, and that's usually solvable by restarting the game.  The game tells you that you won't suffer damage from falling extreme heights, but if you go to certain parts of certain maps you will get insta-killed and there's a cost associated with dying.  You only start with 2 weapon slots and need to progress through the main campaign to unlock all 4.  It's basically impossible to play all of the content without running into balance issues.  There are some ridiculous difficulty spikes, particularly for new players.  There's just a couple parts that can really make you feel underpowered, even if you're several levels ahead of where you should be for that mission.  You're never required to wait for specific times of day, but it can help complete bonus objectives for some missions.  There's no real way to skip to a specific time of day, so you might just have to wait around for 5 minutes until it's night time.  The list of nitpicks like this will likely vary between people in terms of how severely they impact the play experience.

[b]Conclusion[/b]
Ultimately this game is far from pefect as I said way up top.  However, I continue to play it and have spent way too many hours to say that the game is not worth the money or that the flaws outweigh the fun to be had.  For me these annoyances are frustrating and sometimes omnipresent, but are either ignorable in the long run or have slowly transformed into simply being quirks in this already pretty weird game.  This is easy to recommend, as long as you didn't skip to the end and missed the annoyances you will face.

Still one of the best co-op shooters ever made, even years later. Gearbox nailed the "shoot and loot" formula here — the gunplay feels tight and satisfying, and the sheer variety of weapons (millions of them, thanks to the procedural generation system) means you're constantly finding something new and absurd to play with.

What makes it great:

Handsome Jack is one of gaming's all-time great villains — genuinely funny, genuinely menacing, and his commentary throughout the campaign never gets old.
Four distinct playable characters (Axton, Maya, Salvador, Zer0), each with deep skill trees that support very different playstyles. High replay value if you want to try them all.
Co-op is a blast. Drop-in/drop-out multiplayer for up to 4 players makes this one of the best games to play with friends — loot scaling means everyone stays geared up.
The cel-shaded art style has aged beautifully. It doesn't look dated the way a lot of realistic shooters from 2012 do.
Tons of content. Base campaign is meaty, and the DLC (especially Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep) is some of the best expansion content in the genre.
PC performance is excellent — runs smoothly even on modest hardware, and mod support/community tools have kept it fresh.

Minor gripes: Some early-game weapon slog before the good loot starts flowing, and a couple of the DLC side quests feel like padding. Neither comes close to ruining the experience.

If you like looter-shooters, RPG progression, or just want a game with genuine personality and humor, Borderlands 2 is an easy recommend. Get a couple friends, grab the season pass if you can, and go shoot some bandits.

[h1]Borderlands 2: The Best in the Series, Jank and All[/h1]

[h2]TL;DR[/h2]

Borderlands 2 is still my favorite game in the series. Later entries have smoother gunplay, better movement, and plenty of quality-of-life improvements, but none of them put everything together quite as well.

The loot chase is addictive, the Vault Hunters offer genuinely different playstyles, Pandora is packed with memorable content, the DLC is excellent, and Handsome Jack remains the best villain the series has produced.

It is also undeniably janky. Movement feels old, vehicles are awkward, the UI is dated, and the endgame becomes far more restrictive than the campaign.

[b]8/10: Still the best overall Borderlands package for me, even with all the jank.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Combat, Loot & Builds[/h2]

Borderlands 2 understands the satisfaction of finding a gun that immediately makes you rethink your loadout.

Manufacturers feel distinct, elemental damage encourages matching weapons to enemies, and shields, grenade mods, class mods, and relics add plenty of customization. The Vault Hunters are equally important, with action skills and skill trees that support dramatically different playstyles.

[b]The shooting itself has aged more than the systems surrounding it.[/b]

Movement is stiff compared with later entries, weapon handling lacks some modern responsiveness, and enemies occasionally behave strangely. Second Wind also has an incredible ability to make the enemy you need suddenly hide behind something.

None of it ruins the combat. There is simply a layer of 2012 jank covering an otherwise excellent looter-shooter.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Pandora, Quests & Co-op[/h2]

Borderlands 2 massively improves Pandora's variety over the first game. Frozen wastelands, deserts, wildlife preserves, settlements, industrial zones, and Hyperion facilities give the world far more personality.

Side quests are worth doing because they regularly contain memorable characters, ridiculous situations, unique rewards, or additional world-building, even when the objectives themselves are fairly standard.

[b]Co-op is where the Borderlands formula becomes especially difficult to put down.[/b]

Different Vault Hunters and builds working together turn already chaotic encounters into complete nonsense in the best way possible, while the entire game remains perfectly enjoyable solo.

Traversal is weaker. There is plenty of backtracking, some maps are awkward to navigate, and the vehicles have never felt particularly good to control.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Story, Characters & Handsome Jack[/h2]

This is the biggest reason Borderlands 2 still stands above the rest of the series for me.

[b]Handsome Jack is an incredible villain.[/b]

He spends most of the game talking directly to you, mocking your progress while gradually revealing how terrible he actually is. He is funny without being harmless, threatening without becoming generic, and given enough time to become an actual character rather than simply the final boss.

The supporting cast is equally memorable, with Claptrap, Tiny Tina, Scooter, Moxxi, the returning Vault Hunters, and countless side characters giving Pandora enormous personality.

The humor is definitely a product of its era. Some jokes still work perfectly for me, while others have aged exactly how you would expect.

More importantly, the game can become serious when it needs to. Beneath all the stupidity is a surprisingly effective story with characters I genuinely cared about.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Endgame & DLC[/h2]

There is an absurd amount of Borderlands 2 to play. Multiple Vault Hunters, higher difficulties, legendary farming, raid bosses, challenges, optional areas, and years of DLC can easily produce hundreds of hours.

[i]Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep[/i] is the obvious standout, turning Borderlands into a fantasy tabletop adventure while delivering both ridiculous comedy and one of the more emotional stories in the series.

The endgame is where my enthusiasm drops.

Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode pushes enemy health and regeneration hard enough that slag becomes close to mandatory for many builds, while later scaling restricts some of the experimentation that makes the campaign so enjoyable.

[b]I love Borderlands 2's progression far more than I love its highest levels of progression.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Presentation & Final Thoughts[/h2]

The cel-shaded art direction has aged extremely well. Technically, the game clearly comes from the Xbox 360 era, but it still looks distinctly Borderlands.

The jank is much harder to hide. Menus are clunky, physics occasionally lose their mind, enemies do strange things, and legacy features such as PhysX can still cause unnecessary problems on PC.

[b]Borderlands 2 is polished where it matters and held together with duct tape everywhere else.[/b]

Later entries play better, but none of them have matched this combination of loot, builds, world design, co-op, DLC, humor, and memorable characters.

If you want the smoothest Borderlands experience, play one of the newer games. If you want the entry that best represents why people fell in love with the series, this is it.

[b]Borderlands 2 remains the high point of the series, jank and all.[/b]

[b]8/10: Highly recommended.[/b]

[h1]Borderlands 2[/h1]
[b]Rating:[/b] 6/10  A Good Game That Doesn't Quite Match the Memory

[h1]The Short Version[/h1]
[b]Verdict:[/b] Borderlands 2 is a real step up from the first game in most ways that matter, guns feel better, abilities are more fun, loot is more satisfying. But replaying the main campaign now, it doesn't hold up as well as I remembered. Missions feel thin, the areas are just okay, and the whole thing wraps up shorter than I expected.

[table]
[tr][th]Category[/th][th]Verdict[/th][/tr]
[tr][td]Main Campaign[/td][td]Padded With Travel[/td][/tr]
[tr][td]Gunplay & Abilities[/td][td]Big Step Up From BL1[/td][/tr]
[tr][td]Movement & Stability[/td][td]Slow, Some Bugs[/td][/tr]
[tr][td]DLC Content[/td][td]All Over the Place[/td][/tr]
[/table]
[hr][/hr]

[h1]Pandora, Revisited[/h1]
[i]"Still a good game. Just not the one I remembered."[/i]
Going back into the main campaign years later changed how I saw a lot of it. It's not bad, but my biggest issue is how much travel it forces on you, sending you back and forth across areas that take forever to cross for no real reason other than to pad out playtime. The missions themselves rarely rise above fine, and the areas blend together after a while. By the end, the campaign felt shorter than it should have.
[list]
[*] [b]Missions:[/b] Nothing outright bad here, just not much that stuck with me.
[*] [b]Travel:[/b] A lot of forced back-and-forth across areas that take too long to cross, feels like padding more than anything else.
[*] [b]Pacing:[/b] It wrapped up sooner than I expected.
[/list]

[h1]The Guns Talk Louder Than the Story[/h1]
[i]"Everything about the shooting got better. Everything else is a mixed bag."[/i]
This is where Borderlands 2 earns its reputation. The guns feel much better than in the first game, and the abilities stayed fun to use the whole way through. It's a real leap forward from the original. Loot felt good to chase too. Most of my complaints here are about pacing and polish, not the combat itself.
[list]
[*] [b]Gunplay:[/b] A clear improvement over the original.
[*] [b]Abilities:[/b] Worked well and stayed fun.
[*] [b]Movement:[/b] Slower than it needs to be, and missions lean hard on backtracking.
[*] [b]Bugs:[/b] Two missions broke badly enough that we had to restart the whole game to finish them. Annoying, but rare enough that it didn't ruin the run.
[/list]

[h1]The Headhunter Packs: Quick, Cheap, Forgettable[/h1]
[i]"Something to run through, not something to remember."[/i]
The minor DLCs, the full set of Headhunter Packs, were mostly weak. Short, thin on story, and easy to finish in about an hour each. None of them were bad enough to regret, but they didn't earn much enthusiasm either.
[list]
[*] [b]T.K. Baha's Bloody Harvest:[/b] 3/10
[*] [b]The Horrible Hunger of the Ravenous Wattle Gobbler:[/b] 5/10
[*] [b]How Marcus Saved Mercenary Day:[/b] 4/10
[*] [b]Mad Moxxi and the Wedding Day Massacre:[/b] 3/10
[*] [b]Sir Hammerlock vs. the Son of Crawmerax:[/b] 4/10
[/list]

[h1]The Big Four (Plus One)[/h1]
[i]"One of these is actually great. The rest range from fine to skippable."[/i]
The major campaign DLCs varied in quality far more than the base game did. Captain Scarlett's Pirate's Booty has you crossing a big map constantly, with a weak story, though a few missions can be cheesed. Overall it's just okay. Torgue's Campaign of Carnage is a straightforward, kill-everything arena DLC. Not bad, just not memorable. Sir Hammerlock's Big Game Hunt was the low point of the whole game. There's some okay content in there, but most of it falls flat. Then Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep changes gears entirely and it's genuinely good, the one DLC here worth going out of your way for. Commander Lilith & the Fight for Sanctuary ended up shorter and easier than I remembered.
[list]
[*] [b]Captain Scarlett and her Pirate's Booty:[/b] 5/10
[*] [b]Mr. Torgue's Campaign of Carnage:[/b] 4/10
[*] [b]Sir Hammerlock's Big Game Hunt:[/b] 2/10
[*] [b]Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep:[/b] 7/10
[*] [b]Commander Lilith & the Fight for Sanctuary:[/b] 3/10
[/list]

[h1]Pro Tip: Mod It Before You Start[/h1]
[list]
[*] [b]The Tip:[/b] If you want this to feel smoother and more in line with the rest of the series, grab a mod list first: BL2Fix (Flare2V, alienoliver), Borderlands 2 Vulkan support (doitsujin), Better Spawns and Better Travel (juso), AutoPickup (Tominator), Item Lights (Yeti), Loot Collector (Lengyu), LootMarker (juso), Sliding (juso), Storage Manager (Milo), UserFeedback (apple1417), coroutines (juso), tweens (juso), uemath (juso), and Quick Startup (juso, mopioid).
[*] [b]The Benefit:[/b] Fixes a lot of the friction, slow travel, clunky pickups, dated stability, without changing what the game actually is.
[/list]

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
[b]Who is this for?[/b] People who want a real improvement over the first Borderlands and are fine with a campaign that's solid rather than spectacular.

[b]Conclusion:[/b]
Borderlands 2 still holds up. It's just not the classic I remembered it as. The shooting and abilities are a real upgrade, but the campaign is shorter and less memorable than I expected, and the DLC swings hard between forgettable and genuinely great. 6/10, still glad I played it, just not something I'd rush back to.

Hey kiddo, Handsome Jack here. So you want my review of Borderlands 2? Really? You need me to explain why it's one of the greatest games ever made? Okay, fine. Sit down. First off, the guns are great. Like, really great. There are so many guns in this game that you're going to spend half your life picking up a weapon, looking at the numbers, going "Ooooh, 14% more damage," and throwing your perfectly good gun into a garbage pile. That's gameplay, apparently. And you know what? I respect it. The shooting is fantastic, the enemies are fun to kill, the loot is addictive, the characters are memorable, and Pandora is a beautiful little wasteland filled with psychos, murderers, corporations, monsters, and one extremely handsome CEO trying to bring civilization to the place. And yes, I'm talking about myself. You're welcome. Then you've got the Vault Hunters, these four psychopaths who just wander into my perfectly reasonable corporate operation and start murdering my employees. Do you have any idea how much HR paperwork that creates? Seriously. Every time you kill a Hyperion loader, somebody has to file something. Probably. I don't actually read those emails.

And then there's the story, which is where things get interesting. Because apparently I'm the bad guy. Yeah. Sure. The guy trying to clean up Pandora is evil, while the four people walking around shooting literally everything are the heroes. Great logic. Ten out of ten, kiddo. And don't even get me started on the fourth wall. You're sitting there on your couch, holding a controller, thinking you're playing a game, but let's be honest, you aren't. You're working for me now. Congratulations. You spent thirty dollars to become an unpaid Hyperion employee. And you're going to do exactly what I tell you because apparently you enjoy following quest markers. That's adorable. Borderlands 2 is funny, violent, ridiculous, surprisingly emotional, and has enough personality to make most games look like Excel spreadsheets with guns. And just when you're having a good time, the game reminds you that it actually has feelings. People die. Characters suffer. You get sad. Then five minutes later a psycho runs at you screaming about meat. That's range, kiddo. That's art. So yeah, Borderlands 2 gets a 10 out of 10. I'd give it an 11, but apparently the review system only goes to 10. Which is stupid. I checked. It's right there in the code. [h1]Trading Atmosphere for Personality[/h1]

I have a soft spot for the original Borderlands.

Its world felt lonely.

You weren't a legendary hero. You were just another Vault Hunter trying to survive on a planet that seemed determined to turn you into a stain on the rocks. Pandora felt hostile, empty, and dangerous in a way that no other game has quite managed to replicate.

Borderlands 2 leaves that atmosphere behind.

And somehow...

It becomes the better game.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Villain Makes the Difference[/h2]

Handsome Jack doesn't just carry Borderlands 2.

He defines it.

He's funny, charismatic, cruel, and constantly reminds you that he's always one step ahead. Every sarcastic radio call makes defeating him feel a little more personal, and by the end of the game he's become one of gaming's most memorable villains.

Without Jack, Borderlands 2 would still be a good looter shooter.

With him, it's unforgettable.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Everything Feels Better to Play[/h2]

The gunplay is smoother.

The skills are more interesting.

The missions are more varied.

Nearly every system feels like an evolution of what the first game introduced.

The improvements aren't flashy—they're simply everywhere.

It all adds up to a game that's consistently more enjoyable from beginning to end.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]What Was Lost[/h2]

The one thing I still miss is the atmosphere.

Borderlands traded much of its lonely western sci-fi identity for louder humor and a bigger personality.

I understand why.

Most players probably prefer it.

But part of me still misses being just one more expendable Vault Hunter wandering a world that didn't care whether I lived or died.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Borderlands 2 may not be my favorite version of Pandora.

But it's easily the best game in the series.

It refined almost every mechanic, introduced one of gaming's greatest villains, and set a standard the franchise has been chasing ever since.

Borderlands 2 – A Legendary Loot-Filled Adventure That Set the Standard for Co-Op Shooters 🔫💥
🌎 Overview

Some games are remembered because they were successful.

Others are remembered because they changed an entire genre.

Borderlands 2 is one of those games.

Building on the foundation of the original Borderlands, this sequel took everything that made the series unique and improved it in nearly every way.

Bigger worlds.

Better characters.

More creative weapons.

A stronger story.

More memorable moments.

Set on the dangerous planet of Pandora, players take control of a new group of Vault Hunters as they fight against the ruthless dictator Handsome Jack.

What makes Borderlands 2 special is how perfectly it blends RPG progression, first-person shooting, comedy, and cooperative chaos.

Even years later, it remains one of the greatest looter shooters ever created.

⚙️ Gameplay & Mechanics
🔫 The Perfect Looter Shooter Formula

Borderlands 2 takes a simple idea:

Shoot enemies.

Collect loot.

Become stronger.

Repeat.

And turns it into an incredibly addictive gameplay loop.

Every enemy encounter has the potential to reward you with something exciting.

A better weapon.

A rare shield.

A new grenade.

A legendary item.

The constant search for better gear keeps the adventure moving forward.

The shooting feels satisfying, but the RPG elements are what make it unique.

Every level matters.

Every upgrade feels meaningful.

Every new weapon changes how you play.

🧬 Vault Hunters & Character Builds
⭐ Six Unique Playstyles With Endless Possibilities

Borderlands 2 features six playable Vault Hunters, each with their own abilities and skill trees.

🟣 Maya — The Siren

Uses powerful elemental abilities and crowd control through Phaselock.

🔫 Axton — The Commando

Deploys a powerful turret and focuses on tactical combat.

🗡️ Zer0 — The Assassin

A precision-based character built around stealth and critical damage.

🥊 Salvador — The Gunzerker

Can dual-wield weapons and create absolute destruction.

🤖 Gaige — The Mechromancer

Uses Deathtrap, a powerful robotic companion.

💀 Krieg — The Psycho

A chaotic melee-focused character built around aggression.

Each character can be built in multiple ways, making every playthrough feel different.

Experimenting with skills, weapons, and gear combinations is one of the game's biggest strengths.

💥 Weapons & Loot
⭐ Billions of Guns, Endless Possibilities

The weapon system is where Borderlands 2 truly shines.

Every gun has personality.

You can find weapons that:

🔥 Set enemies on fire.

⚡ Shock shields instantly.

🧊 Freeze opponents.

💣 Launch explosive rounds.

🏆 One of the Best Villains in Gaming

The story is one of Borderlands 2's greatest improvements.

At the center of everything is Handsome Jack, one of gaming's most memorable villains.

He is funny.

Charismatic.

Cruel.

Completely unpredictable.

Every interaction with him adds personality to the story.

The game balances comedy with genuine emotional moments, creating a campaign that is much more memorable than players expected from a chaotic shooter.

The supporting cast is also excellent, with characters that remain iconic years later.

🌎 World Design
🪐 Pandora Has Never Felt Bigger

Pandora is filled with unique environments, enemies, and secrets.

Players explore:

🏜️ Desert wastelands.

❄️ Frozen landscapes.

🏭 Industrial areas.

🌋 Dangerous alien locations.

Each area has its own personality and atmosphere.

The world is colorful, strange, and full of surprises.

The environments are not just backgrounds—they are filled with quests, hidden loot, and memorable encounters.

⚔️ Combat & Enemies
🔥 Fast, Explosive, and Addictive

Combat in Borderlands 2 is pure chaos.

Enemies come in many forms, forcing players to constantly adjust their strategy.

You might fight:

🛡️ Armored enemies.

👾 Alien creatures.

🤖 Robots.

💀 Bandits.

Every fight feels different because your weapons and abilities change how you approach combat.

The game rewards experimentation.

There is no single correct way to play.

🎨 Visuals & Presentation
🎨 A Comic Book World Full of Personality

The cel-shaded art style remains one of Borderlands' greatest strengths.

Borderlands 2 looks unique even today.

The colors are bright.

The characters are exaggerated.

The world is full of personality.

Instead of chasing realism, the game creates an unforgettable visual identity.

Every location feels like a comic book brought to life.

🔊 Sound & Atmosphere
🎵 A Perfect Mix of Humor and Action

The sound design matches the game's personality perfectly.

Weapons sound powerful.

Characters are full of energy.

The soundtrack enhances the excitement of exploring Pandora.

The writing and voice acting are especially impressive, helping create a world that feels alive.

🌐 Multiplayer & Replayability
🤝 The Ultimate Co-Op Experience

Borderlands 2 is at its best with friends.

Four players.

Different characters.

Thousands of weapons.

Endless combinations.

Co-op creates unforgettable moments.

One player freezes enemies.

Another destroys everything with rockets.

Another keeps the team alive.

The teamwork possibilities are endless.

With multiple characters, difficulty modes, DLC expansions, and legendary gear to hunt, Borderlands 2 offers hundreds of hours of replayability.

✅ What It Does Brilliantly

Endless replayability.

Borderlands 2 succeeds because it understands the most important part of a looter shooter:

The journey matters.

It is not just about reaching the strongest level.

It is about the moments along the way.

Finding your first legendary weapon.

Laughing at a ridiculous mission.

Beating a difficult boss with friends.

Discovering a completely broken weapon combination.

Those moments are why players keep returning to Pandora.

It improved everything from the original game while delivering a story, villain, and cast of characters that are still remembered today.

The gameplay loop is addictive.

The humor is memorable.

The loot is endless.

Even years later, few games capture the same feeling of discovering something amazing with friends.

Borderlands 2 gives you so many guns that eventually you stop asking "Is this a good weapon?" and start asking "Does this shotgun shoot swords, electricity, or both?" The answer is usually "yes." Then Handsome Jack shows up, insults you over the radio, and suddenly you're fueled entirely by spite. Absolute chaos, and somehow it all works.

Another excellent game. The concept of an semi-open-world loot shooter with a big story line and tons of side quests and plots is incredible.

The execution itself is great too! Graphics, audio, level design and difficulty are very well made, especially when considering that this game was released in 2012. Only 1-2 side missions and the arena side quests are unproportionally difficult, but the main story does not suffer any unfair challenges.
What stood out to me the most is the gameplay and the depth of your weapons and skills. Not only do you have multiple different classes that you can choose from. But, you encounter tons of unique weapons, some with special abilities and creative (dis-)advantages. Additionally, you can improve one skill with each level-up and pick small perks whenever you fulfill a little achievement. This is neatly put into separate little menus, which don't overwhelm you upon opening :)

The only two actual problems I had were with me getting stuck in some corners occasionally and the humor being quite outdated. Some jokes are just flat-out old, while some aren't funny at all. This may be personal preference, but I had to cringe at a few jokes because they were so flat.

However, I don't believe that this takes away from the overall charm this game brings and I might consider buying newer titles as well due to the concept being almost perfectly carried out. But, before buying you might consider about if you want to back 2K as they position themselves against the "Stop Killing Games" campaign, which advocates for greater consumer rights when it comes to video games.

[h1]Borderlands 2[/h1]
[h3]Amazing FPS with Misunderstood Changes [/h3]
[h3]Really worth trying![/h3]

Borderlands 2 is arguably one of the best sequels ever made, improving upon every aspect of its predecessor. The exploration is excellent, gunplay is really fun, the story is engaging, and the game's progression is even more balanced than in the previous entry. Unfortunately, the game gained a very poor reputation due to changes made to its EULA (End User License Agreement), as well as the wave of misinformation that followed. Much of the criticism came from people who never took the time to properly read or understand those changes. 

Many of these changes regarding the game's terms of use are not actually new. For example, the enforcement of restrictions against mod creators who attempt to profit from modifications or the unauthorized use of the game's assets has been common practice for years. Speaking with members of the modding community about this issue quickly shows how irrelevant this change for new and veteran users actually is. 

Regarding the spyware allegations, this company had been collecting gameplay statistics and certain basic user data well before the update. These changes did not introduce the practice of data collection itself, which had already existed in some form for years. With those points clarified, we can finally focus on the game itself. 

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
Like its predecessor, this sequel includes RPG mechanics centered around loot, weapons, and character development. This is complemented by an elemental system of strengths and weaknesses, where the effectiveness of a weapon or attack depends on its elemental type. Certain elements deal more damage to specific enemies, while others are less effective. This approach is both intuitive and engaging, and its influence can still be seen in many modern games today.

The combat is highly enjoyable, as the game offers a wide variety of weapons, abilities, and character builds, allowing for extensive customization to suit any playstyle. Overall, the game is extremely engaging, constantly encouraging progression through rewarding gameplay and story advancement.

Aiming is another aspect that has been improved in this sequel. It feels more comfortable and intuitive thanks to the wider variety of sights and scopes available on the new weapons, making the gunplay both more enjoyable and more consistent. 

[h3]Art and World Design[/h3]
The game uses a cel-shaded art style for its character models, environments, weapons, and other visual assets, giving it a distinctive and timeless appearance. Within this style, the characters, enemies, and environments feature designs full of life and personality, reflecting the exaggerated and rebellious aesthetic that was characteristic of many games from that era.

The world of Borderlands 2 is superior to that of the first game in many ways. Its main antagonist is actually well defined, with a charismatic personality, clear motivations and a constant presence throughout the story, making him far more memorable and relevant to the overall narrative. Also, more interesting subplots are introduced, helping to expand the game’s lore of its characters, cities and clans.

[h3]Music and Sound effects[/h3]
The soundtrack is just as good as the one in the first game, with a great selection of action and suspense tracks that complement both the quiet moments of exploration and the more intense combat encounters.

Borderlands 2 – 10/10 – The King of Looter-Shooters
Borderlands 2 is a game that defined a generation of looter-shooters and still feels like a masterpiece over a decade later. Released in 2012 by Gearbox Software, this sequel takes everything great about the original and cranks it up to absurd, hilarious, and endlessly replayable levels. With its signature cel-shaded art style, addictive gunplay, unforgettable characters, and a massive world packed with secrets, Borderlands 2 isn’t just a great game—it’s a benchmark for the genre. It perfectly blends shooter action with deep RPG progression, dark humor, and co-op mayhem in a way that few titles have matched since.
One of the standout features of Borderlands 2 is its incredible gunplay and absurd variety of weapons. The game famously boasts “over a bazillion guns,” and the hype is real. Every weapon feels distinct thanks to randomized parts, unique effects, and wild manufacturer traits—Jakobs guns feel like powerful revolvers from a Western, while Maliwan weapons spit elemental death with style. Whether you’re a commando summoning a turret, a siren phasing through enemies, a gunzerker dual-wielding everything, or an assassin picking off foes from the shadows, each of the six Vault Hunters offers a completely different playstyle. The moment-to-moment combat is fast, fluid, and ridiculously satisfying, especially when you start melting bosses with perfectly rolled legendaries.
The single-player campaign (which is even better with friends) follows a new group of Vault Hunters as they take on the tyrannical Handsome Jack and the Hyperion Corporation. The story is genuinely engaging, filled with sharp writing, memorable villains, and laugh-out-loud moments. Pandora is a living, breathing wasteland full of quirky NPCs, hidden Easter eggs, and side quests that often rival the main story in quality. The world feels massive and alive, with distinct regions ranging from frozen tundras to toxic swamps and bandit-filled badlands. The humor—equal parts crude, clever, and chaotic—elevates the entire experience and keeps you smiling even during the hundreds of hours you’ll sink into it.
Multiplayer is where Borderlands 2 ascends to legendary status. Drop-in, drop-out co-op for up to four players turns the game into an absolute riot. Split-screen, online, or LAN—however you play, the game scales beautifully. Farming bosses, sharing loot, tackling raid bosses, and screaming at each other during intense fights creates some of the best co-op memories in gaming. The endgame is incredibly deep with the Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode, countless DLCs (many of which are outstanding), and an endless grind for perfect gear that never gets old.
Visually, the cel-shaded style has aged like fine wine. It still looks vibrant, distinctive, and stylish today, avoiding the dated realism trap that plagues many older shooters. The environments are packed with detail, the animations are punchy, and the particle effects during big fights are pure eye candy. The sound design and soundtrack are equally excellent, with a killer licensed soundtrack and voice acting that brings every character to life (especially Handsome Jack—easily one of the best villains in gaming).
What makes Borderlands 2 earn a perfect score is how complete and generous it feels. It constantly rewards you with better gear, fun new builds, and hilarious writing. The DLC expansions (especially Tiny Tina’s Assault on Dragon Keep) are some of the strongest ever released. There’s very little to criticize here—occasional balance quirks or repetitive enemy types feel like minor nitpicks in an otherwise flawless package.
10/10 – Chaotic, Hilarious, and Timeless
Borderlands 2 remains the gold standard for looter-shooters. It delivers an unbeatable mix of addictive gameplay, endless loot, memorable storytelling, and pure co-op joy that still pulls players back in years later. Whether you’re playing solo or with a full squad, it’s a wild ride across Pandora that never fails to entertain. If you’ve never experienced it, you’re missing out on one of the most fun games ever made. Hands down, a must-play classic.

Borderlands 2 is easily one of the greatest video games ever made.  I've played it ever since it released on the Xbox 360 all the way back in 2012.  Its story, writing, sound design, music, and gameplay are nearly perfect and flawless.  Handsome Jack is singlehandedly my favorite villain of all time, and yes I will go out on a limb and say he's better than GLaDOS, Darth Vader, the Joker, or Hannibal Lecter.  Jack is the twisted, egomaniacal, beating heart of Borderlands 2's story and one of the central reasons why it works.

Borderlands 2's writing does such a spectacular job at knowing when to be the most hilariously comedic game ever released and when to stop pulling its punches with extremely dour, dark, and serious plot points.  This game, from the voice lines and sounds of each playable character and every enemy you encounter to the art style to the gun manufacturers themselves and how each of their weapons behave, oozes and overflows with personality like no other FPS.  Aside from Handsome Jack, so many other characters in this game are well-written, including Tiny Tina, Brick, Mordecai, Scooter, Ellie, Sir Hammerlock, and of course Claptrap to name just a few.  And aside from their gameplay, the main cast of playable characters, Axton, Salvador, Maya, Zer0, Krieg, and Gaige, are all wonderfully written and voiced as well.  

They also have some of the best RPG-class designs in any game released.  Each of the playable characters have unique and extatically fun abilities with engrossing skill/perk trees.  I'm not sure why Far Cry 3 was dubbed "Skyrim with guns" when Borderlands 2 has been the holder of that title ever since.  Destiny and Fallout are a joke compared to how superior Borderlands 2 is as an RPG looter-shooter.  The character classes of Borderlands 2 are the mightiest in the entire franchise and are the reason why it's gameplay is so unbelievably legendary and addicting.  While I'm personally not a fan of Maya's gameplay, no other FPS experience will match that of Salvador, Zer0, or Krieg.  None.

Unfortunately, the weakest portions of Borderlands 2 are two of its central gameplay mechanics, but they aren't bad by any means and certainly not enough to prevent me from returning to this gem.  The gunplay is inconsistent.  Many firearms are fun, punchy, imposing, and satisfying to use, but towards higher levels assault rifles and SMG's are outclassed by pistols, shotguns, snipers, and rocket launchers, and their recoil and aiming stability has to be one of the worst designed in any FPS I've played.  It's not that Borderlands 2 has to be "realistic" when it comes to weapon design, but as a real-life gun owner and firearms enthusiast, it's just frustrating to see assault rifles and SMG's so poorly engage targets at mid to longer ranges because the aiming and recoil patterns of them shake in a stupid cross-cut swaying motion, rather than a predictable pull upwards.  Their damage is likewise pathetic compared to other weapon types and the other main reason why their design is so pitiful. 

The second weakest gameplay mechanic of Borderlands 2 is the level scaling past level 50.  At least for me personally, I refuse to play Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode.  Enemies are far too punishing and just about every single one becomes a bullet sponge forcing players into far too restrictive optimal playstyles.  Other than the gunplay and post-level 50 combat, everything else about the gameplay is grand slam perfect.  Enemy types and environmental level designs are extremely diverse and challenging in their own unique ways.  It's a gargantuan shame that later entries in the Borderlands franchise largely fixed my issues with the gunplay but then ruined everything else that made Borderlands 2 its peak installment.  Music is largely hit or miss.  Some tracks are mildly irritating in how bland and uninteresting they are, while others are some that I still listen to this day.  This game somehow combines Western cowboy, sci-fi space digital age, Mad Max, and military war themes in its story, gameplay, and music all in one beautiful, gory, zany concoction, and I absolutely love it.

If you've read this far into my review and still have not begun downloading Borderlands 2, stop reading and just buy the damn game already.  It is worth every single penny, and you won't regret it one bit!

[h1]Adventures of the Smart Patrol[/h1]

It turns out that a unique presentation can go a long way in making your Action RPG/FPS hybrid into a smash hit. Borderlands was a surprise hit, so naturally Gearbox goes ahead and makes a sequel. Give the people what they liked about the original but Bigger! Better! Badder! and so on. And for a game that doesn't really make a dramatic change to the formula its surprising just how much better it feels compared to the first game.

I think one of the more interesting things about Borderlands 2 is the usage of bullet speed as a way to make guns feel different. Granted i'm pretty sure that even in the first game that guns were hit-scan, but its much more noticeable in the second game. It does a lot in making each weapon feel different, especially with how weapon brands have become more distinctive, with each manufacturer not only biasing towards a given stat but actively changing how each gun is used (Jakob's guns are semi-auto with high firing rates, Torgue guns deal explosive damage but fire slowly etc.).

Moreover the move away from the largely desert setting of the first game towards a greater variance in biomes is really welcome. for all the focus on cell-shading that B1 was famous for, its kinda shocking how brown the game is (as was the style of the time). Borderlands 2 by contrast is awash in color - its telling how the game starts in an arctic setting just to hit home that Pandora is more than just a bunch of brown dirt with patches of dark red blood. The game looks really good on an OLED display at 4K, which can't be said about a lot of games from this period!

From this perspective it seems that Borderlands 2 is a pretty typical sequel in the best possible way - the stuff you love from the first game but with little tweaks that end up making the experience greater than the whole. And honestly i had a good time with it. If for some reason you haven't played it before its worth giving a shot. however...

[h1]Mr DNA[/h1]

I briefly looked at the wikipedia page for Borderlands 2 and the production section points out that Gearbox wanted to give the sequel more of an actual storyline. To be honest, Borderlands 1 was very thin on the ground when it came to narrative. A lot of the game is spent being told where to go next and the Crimson Lance kinda show up too late to have any impact. That's not really a big issue, especially since the plot largely stays out of the way. The writing in the sequel, by contrast, is atrocious and there's a lot more of it. There's a greater focus on character motivation and development that I never cared about (with multiple character deaths!) and it all feels like a waste. 

However the real killing blow comes from the attempts at comedy. Gearbox hired Youtuber Anthony Burch to be the lead writer and quite frankly I'm shocked YouTube comedians were still allowed to enter game development after this. To be fair, i think some of my reaction is mainly due to the fact that the game is 14 years old and the jokes have dated very badly. To put it another way, the comedy feels like the patient zero for what i can best describe as 'redditor' humor: Lots of references, snarky quips (including a few 'That just happened!'), jokes that go on for a little too long. The only thing missing is a reference to bacon. A special mention should go out to Tiny Tina, wherein the actress (Burch's sister Ashley - by all accounts she is a talented actor so I won't hold it against her) puts on a mannerism that can only be described as 'white girl you can't be talking like that'. Its so bad that from what i've heard they changed her characterization in the DLCs and sequels. 

And then there's Handsome Jack. Fun fact: Anthony Burch has said that he based the character on himself. I hope to god he is not being totally serious because good lord. They're clearly going for the witty antagonist who you love to hate, but every time he shows up I just want him to shut up. It's been a while since i played Portal so IDK how well that game's writing holds up but Jack is just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ version of GlaDoS without the charm. It really brings down a game that can otherwise be very enjoyable.

- Great characterization of returning characters (Roland in particular)

- Slag was a nice idea to try and add another dimension to fights
- Axton is a great expansion onto Roland's skill tree from the first game (I mained Roland)
- Maya is a great support class, and other characters have support elements in their skills
- There is no better feeling than using a sniper to cross-map a downed ally with phaselock-revive

Cons:
- Gun selection/spawns are lacking compared to Borderlands 1 (non-unique ones)
- Gunplay heavily favors certain weapon types across all classes (BL1 was class specific, at least)
- Questlines keep you in biomes for extended periods, which is sometimes fine, sometimes not

- Lot of backtracking in map design, not many cramped/close quarter areas like in the first game
